items.readable_text:
Content:
Rational functions have infinite limits when the [MATH: x]-value approaches vertical asymptotes. To find the infinite limits of a rational function [MATH: f(x),] we first find the vertical asymptotes.

Content:
For example, consider the rational function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-2}.] This rational function has a vertical asymptote at [MATH: x=2.]

Content:
To find the one-sided limits at the asymptote [MATH: x=2,] we check the sign of [MATH: f(x)] as [MATH: x] approaches [MATH: 2] from the left and the right.

Content:
- To find the limit as [MATH: x \to 2^-,] we evaluate [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x]-values very close to [MATH: x=2] from the left:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 1.9] | [MATH: 1.99] | [MATH: 1.999] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: -10] | [MATH: -100] | [MATH: -1\,000] |

Content:
The values of [MATH: f(x)] are negative, and they get more and more negative. Therefore, [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = -\infty.]

Content:
- To find the limit as [MATH: x \to 2^+,] we evaluate [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x]-values very close to [MATH: x=2] from the right:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 2.1] | [MATH: 2.01] | [MATH: 2.001] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: 10] | [MATH: 100] | [MATH: 1\,000] |

Content:
The values of [MATH: f(x)] are positive, and they get larger and larger. Therefore, [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = +\infty.]

Content:

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 3^+} \dfrac{1}{x^2-x-6}.]
sections.readable_text: Evaluate [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 3^+} \dfrac{1}{x^2-x-6}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that we can factor the function, as follows:

[MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x^2-x-6} = \dfrac{1}{(x-3)(x+2)}]

So, the function [MATH: f(x)] has two vertical asymptotes, [MATH: x=-2] and [MATH: x=3.]

Since [MATH: x=3] is a vertical asymptote, the limit as [MATH: x \to 3^+] will be either [MATH: +\infty] or [MATH: -\infty.]

To find the limit as [MATH: x \to 3^+,] we evaluate [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x]-values very close to [MATH: x=3] from the right:

This implies that the function [MATH: f(x)] has two vertical asymptotes, [MATH: x=-2] and [MATH: x=1.]

sections.normalized_html:
Given that [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x}{(x-1)^2},] which of the following statements is correct?

  1. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 1^-}f(x)= -\infty]

  2. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 1^+} f(x)= +\infty]

  3. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 1} f(x)= +\infty]
sections.readable_text:
Given that [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x}{(x-1)^2},] which of the following statements is correct?

1. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 1^-}f(x)= -\infty]
2. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 1^+} f(x)= +\infty]
3. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 1} f(x)= +\infty]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The function [MATH: f(x)= \dfrac{x}{(x-1)^2}] has a vertical asymptote at [MATH: x=1.]

To compute the one-sided limits as [MATH: x \to 1,] we evaluate [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x]-values very close to [MATH: x=1] from the right and from the left.

[MATH: x]

[MATH: 0.9]

[MATH: 0.99]

[MATH: 1]

[MATH: 1.01]

[MATH: 1.1]

[MATH: f(x)]

[MATH: 90]

[MATH: 9\,900]

[MATH: \text{undefined}]

[MATH: 10\,100]

[MATH: 110]

All the values of [MATH: f(x)] are positive, and they get larger and larger as [MATH: x\to1] from both sides. Therefore,

[MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 1^-} f(x)=\lim\limits_{x \to 1^+} f(x)= +\infty.]

Consequently, statement I is false and II is true.

Finally, since both left and right-sided limits at [MATH: x=1] are equal, we have [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 1} f(x)= +\infty,]

and therefore III is true.

In conclusion, only statements II and III are true. A plot of the function is shown below.

sections.normalized_html:
Given that [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{2-x}{x^2-4},] which of the following statements is correct?

  1. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to (-2)^+}f(x)= -\infty]

  2. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 2^+}f(x)= -\infty]

  3. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 2^-}f(x)= \infty]
sections.readable_text:
Given that [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{2-x}{x^2-4},] which of the following statements is correct?

1. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to (-2)^+}f(x)= -\infty]
2. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 2^+}f(x)= -\infty]
3. [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 2^-}f(x)= \infty]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's factor the numerator and denominator, as follows: [MATH: f(x)|= (2 − x)/(x^{2} − 4); = − ((x − 2))/((x − 2)(x + 2))]

Therefore, the domain is [MATH: x\neq \pm 2], and we notice that the function can be simplified: [MATH: f(x) = − (1)/(x + 2)]

Now we see that the function has only one vertical asymptote, [MATH: x=-2.] So statements II and III are false.

To find [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to (-2)^+}f(x),] we evaluate [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x]-values very close to [MATH: x=-2] from the right.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Rational functions have infinite limits when the [MATH: x]-value approaches vertical asymptotes. To find the infinite limits of a rational function [MATH: f(x),] we first find the vertical asymptotes.

Content:
For example, consider the rational function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-2}.] This rational function has a vertical asymptote at [MATH: x=2.]

Content:
To find the one-sided limits at the asymptote [MATH: x=2,] we check the sign of [MATH: f(x)] as [MATH: x] approaches [MATH: 2] from the left and the right.

Content:
- To find the limit as [MATH: x \to 2^-,] we evaluate [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x]-values very close to [MATH: x=2] from the left:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 1.9] | [MATH: 1.99] | [MATH: 1.999] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: -10] | [MATH: -100] | [MATH: -1\,000] |

Content:
The values of [MATH: f(x)] are negative, and they get more and more negative. Therefore, [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = -\infty.]

Content:
- To find the limit as [MATH: x \to 2^+,] we evaluate [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x]-values very close to [MATH: x=2] from the right:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 2.1] | [MATH: 2.01] | [MATH: 2.001] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: 10] | [MATH: 100] | [MATH: 1\,000] |

Content:
The values of [MATH: f(x)] are positive, and they get larger and larger. Therefore, [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = +\infty.]

Content:
These one-sided limits match up with what we see in the graph of [MATH: f(x),] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1f0de881aee9cf164ae6f91299a59145]

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating the Right-Sided Limit of a Rational Function at a Vertical Asymptote

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 3^+} \dfrac{1}{x^2-x-6}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that we can factor the function, as follows:

[MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x^2-x-6} = \dfrac{1}{(x-3)(x+2)}]

So, the function [MATH: f(x)] has two vertical asymptotes, [MATH: x=-2] and [MATH: x=3.]

Since [MATH: x=3] is a vertical asymptote, the limit as [MATH: x \to 3^+] will be either [MATH: +\infty] or [MATH: -\infty.]

To find the limit as [MATH: x \to 3^+,] we evaluate [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x]-values very close to [MATH: x=3] from the right:

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 3.1] | [MATH: 3.01] | [MATH: 3.001] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: \approx 1.96] | [MATH: \approx 19.96] | [MATH: \approx 199.96] |

The values of [MATH: f(x)] are positive, and they get larger and larger. Therefore,
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 3^+} f(x) = +\infty.]

This matches up with what we see in the graph of [MATH: f(x),] shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/699affabb0d7d5f074de07be10a3540c]

Item 5 — Example: Evaluating the Left-Sided Limit of a Rational Function at a Vertical Asymptote

This implies that the function [MATH: f(x)] has two vertical asymptotes, [MATH: x=-2] and [MATH: x=1.]

Since [MATH: x=1] is a vertical asymptote, the limit as [MATH: x \to 1^-] will be either [MATH: +\infty] or [MATH: -\infty.]

To find the limit is [MATH: x \to 1^-,] we evaluate [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x]-values very close to [MATH: x=1] from the left:

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 0.9] | [MATH: 0.99] | [MATH: 0.999] |

The values of [MATH: f(x)] are negative, and they get more and more negative. Therefore,
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 1^-} f(x)= -\infty.]

Item 8 — Example: Identifying Correct Limits of a Given Rational Function

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The function [MATH: f(x)= \dfrac{x}{(x-1)^2}] has a vertical asymptote at [MATH: x=1.]

To compute the one-sided limits as [MATH: x \to 1,] we evaluate [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x]-values very close to [MATH: x=1] from the right and from the left.

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 0.9] | [MATH: 0.99] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1.01] | [MATH: 1.1] |

All the values of [MATH: f(x)] are positive, and they get larger and larger as [MATH: x\to1] from both sides. Therefore,

[MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 1^-} f(x)=\lim\limits_{x \to 1^+} f(x)= +\infty.]

Consequently, statement I is false and II is true.

Finally, since both left and right-sided limits at [MATH: x=1] are equal, we have
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to 1} f(x)= +\infty,]

and therefore III is true.

In conclusion, only statements II and III are true. A plot of the function is shown below.
